summary: A statement by the Internet Architecture Board on the architectural issues raised by internationalizing domain names. It is not a protocol specification. It tries to clarify the range of problems that arise. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: People want web addresses in their own alphabets. The architecture board explains why that is trickier than it sounds, since many programs share the same names.

questions: iab statement on i18n domain names
why is internationalizing domain names hard
subtitle: The architectural challenges of putting languages into web addresses.

tldr.problem: As the Internet expands globally, users want to use their own languages and character sets in domain names. However, domain names are used by protocols across national boundaries, creating risk of isolated network segments.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB analyzes the architectural issues and technical challenges that arise when internationalizing domain names, examining impacts on email, routing, network management, and security.
tldr.outcome: No solution is attempted here; the document emphasizes that any internationalization approach must preserve global interoperability and avoid creating isolated islands of communication.

today: RFC 2825 is an informational statement and has not been obsoleted. It remains relevant as a description of the architectural challenges that internationalization efforts must address.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2825 is a statement by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) on the challenges of internationalizing domain names. The goal of internationalization is to let users around the world express themselves, write names, and navigate the network using their own languages and character sets. This directly impacts domain names used in email addresses and web URLs.

However, domain names are used by protocols that operate across national and organizational boundaries. Unlike standalone applications that can be deployed everywhere simultaneously, Internet protocols must maintain worldwide interoperability. The IAB emphasizes that solutions must avoid isolating regions or communities from the rest of the global network.
sections.plainLanguage: People all over the world want to type web addresses in their own languages, not just English. But the Internet connects everyone together, so any change has to work everywhere at once.

sections.title: A Definition of Success
sections.content:
The IAB establishes that successful internationalization of domain names must be evaluated not just on technical features alone, but on its total impact on the Internet and end-users. Solutions must not isolate users from their global neighbors, even if they solve a local problem.

The challenge is that existing Internet protocols have character restrictions. Some protocols, like email (SMTP and MIME), do not allow the full range of characters that DNS specifications permit. Additionally, implementations of core Internet protocols sometimes do not implement all options that standards allow. These practical limitations mean solutions must be compatible with real deployments, not just theoretical standards.
sections.plainLanguage: A good solution must work with all the old programs and systems that are already running everywhere. You can't break something just to add a new feature.

sections.title: Challenges Across the Internet Stack
sections.content:
The document outlines specific interoperability problems that internationalized domain names would encounter across multiple Internet services. Email systems are a critical issue: protocols like SMTP and MIME restrict characters in the domain portion of addresses. Some email software is known to fail, discard, or misdirect mail when it encounters non-ASCII domain names. Until most email servers worldwide are upgraded, email delivery would break for internationalized domains.

Similar problems exist in routing (RPSL uses DNS naming rules), network management (SNMP implementations rarely handle internationalized names), and security systems (TLS certificates and IPsec both rely on traditional domain name matching). When a TLS client validates a server certificate containing an internationalized domain name against the server name used to reach it, improper comparison could either reject legitimate connections or accept forged ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Email, routing, and security systems all depend on domain names in some way. If you change how domain names work, all of these might break unless they are updated too.

sections.title: Deployment Reality and Security Implications
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that deployment takes many years. New protocols and enhancements typically spread unevenly across the Internet, with some regions and systems adopting change much faster than others. If internationalization solutions were deployed before all dependent systems are ready, they could create islands of interoperation that isolate early adopters from the rest of the network.

Additionally, non-standard name assignments, if deployed in response to pressures for national character set representation, could result in names that are not globally unique. This opens the possibility of spoofing attacks, where a host in one domain could impersonate a host in another due to name collisions (see RFC 2826 on DNS root issues).
sections.plainLanguage: If different countries set up their own Internet systems without agreeing on names, you could end up with the same address meaning different things in different places. This breaks the entire Internet.

sections.title: Conclusion and Next Steps
sections.content:
Although many ways exist to assign internationalized names that are compatible with modern DNS, not all are compatible with the full range of necessary networking tools. The effects on existing Internet systems must be carefully evaluated before deployment.

Some proposed solutions would cause Internet communications to fail in hard-to-detect ways, creating problems for both those who deploy them and those who do not. The IAB identifies the IDN Working Group as the appropriate forum for identifying and discussing solutions that maintain global interoperability while achieving visible-name representation in users' own languages.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding a solution is hard, but important. The people working on this need to make sure any change they make works with everything else on the Internet.
